keyVerseText: Unto the woman he said, I will greatly multiply thy sorrow and thy conception; in sorrow thou shalt bring forth children; and thy desire shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee. to thy: or, subject to thy husband
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun עִצָּבוֹן (ʻitstsâbôwn) derives from the root עָצַב (ʻâtsab), which primarily means to carve or fashion, but carries a secondary, figurative sense of causing pain, grief, or vexation. This root suggests a process of shaping that involves struggle or hardship, implying that the sorrow and toil encapsulated by עִצָּבוֹן are not merely emotional states but are deeply connected to the experience of laborious effort and distress. Thus, the root adds a dimension of both physical and emotional shaping through pain, going beyond a simple English translation of sorrow or toil.
usageInScripture: The word עִצָּבוֹן appears three times in Scripture, consistently conveying themes of sorrow, pain, and toil. Its top translations—'thy sorrow,' 'for thy sake in sorrow,' and 'and toil'—highlight a close relationship between emotional distress and physical labor or hardship. This consistency underscores the term’s dual emphasis on both the burdensome toil and the accompanying sorrow, often linked to human experience under divine judgment or the fallen condition.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding עִצָּבוֹן enriches our grasp of human suffering as portrayed in Scripture, revealing it as both a consequence of the Fall and a part of the divine ordering of life. The root’s connection to shaping and fashioning through pain points to the refining and formative aspects of toil and sorrow in the believer’s journey. It reminds Christians that suffering is not merely punitive but can also serve a purpose in God's providential plan. Recognizing this word’s depth encourages faith in God’s sovereignty over hardship and invites believers to trust in His redemptive work through Christ, who bore ultimate sorrow and toil for our salvation.
keyVerseReflection: In Genesis 3:16, God declares to the woman, 'I will greatly multiply thy sorrow and thy conception; in sorrow thou shalt bring forth children.' Here, עִצָּבוֹן conveys the intensified pain and labor associated with childbirth as part of the curse following the Fall. The word deepens our understanding of the verse by emphasizing not only physical toil but also the accompanying emotional sorrow, highlighting the profound impact of sin on human experience. This sorrowful toil serves as a reminder of the brokenness in the world and the need for redemption.
